note:
ISO 2026-W23 runs from June 1 through June 7. Ceres and Uranus are separated by about 0.8° in geocentric ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot.

**Naked eye:** No principal lunar phase is listed this week. Check the Moon's position each night and favor darker hours for low-contrast targets. Use Epsilon Cen, Alkaid as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -12.4; direct motion; 99.5% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Pluto in ecliptic longitude Jun 05 00:21 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude -0.5; direct motion; 70.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -3.9; direct motion; 79.5% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 1.3; direct motion; 96.5% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Ceres: In solar glare; magnitude 8.8; direct motion; 99.9% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Uranus in ecliptic longitude Jun 03 08:33 UTC. Jupiter: Naked eye; magnitude -1.9; direct motion; 99.6% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.9; direct motion; 99.8% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Uranus: In solar glare; magnitude 5.8; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Ceres in ecliptic longitude Jun 03 08:33 UTC. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.8; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.5; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Jun 05 00:21 UTC.

**Binoculars:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified for binocular observing this week.

**Small telescope:** Southern Pinwheel: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; NGC 5248: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M3: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; NGC 5286: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

**Substantial telescope:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified as requiring a substantial telescope this week.

story_candidates.dek: Southern Pinwheel is an observing target in Hya carried by the weekly Calendar.
story_candidates.body:
Why it is here: The Calendar selected Southern Pinwheel as one of this week’s fixed-sky observing targets.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Hya constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

story_candidates.dek: Fixed object 969 is a star in Cen; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 13h 39m and declination -53.5°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star does not rise above the geometric horizon. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Cen constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.

story_candidates.dek: Alkaid is a star in UMa; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 13h 47m and declination +49.3°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star is circumpolar (at 45° declination it touches the geometric horizon at lower culmination). It reaches approximately 86° altitude at upper culmination. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved UMa constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.
